endorsements.quote: Institutional review boards should consider algorithm registration a prerequisite for approval, and scientific journals could make registration a condition for publication, continuing a tradition of rigorous scientific accountability, as has been done in the past 5.

While guidelines like SPIRIT-AI 10,C O N S O R T - A I11, and DECIDE-AI 12 promote algorithmic information reporting in scientific publications for transparency, they lack specific requirements to translate principles into practice13.

unlisted_practices: Establish a mandatory, publicly accessible registry for early-stage clinical AI algorithms, administered by a non-profit organization, with unique identifiers, audit trail, and linkage to trial and device identifiers.
Register AI algorithms before clinical deployment and before submitting a trial protocol for ethics approval.
Disclose general algorithm information, including model development, training and validation datasets, and clinical performance, while protecting IP and not requiring source code sharing.

Update the AI algorithm registration after substantial model changes such as retraining on new data or altered algorithmic processing, and periodically report updated performance metrics for models with active learning or frequent updates.
Healthcare institutions should require early algorithm registration as a prerequisite even when not subject to regulatory oversight.

Generative AI registration should document foundation model type, version, manufacturer, training data corpus, fine-tuning or grounding process, and policies preventing dissemination of sensitive input data into foundation models.
Governments, international organizations, AI experts, and the private sector should collaborate to facilitate and regulate an AI algorithm registry.

screen.reason: This is a perspective/commentary paper advocating for early-stage AI algorithm registration and registry creation to enhance trust and transparency in healthcare AI.
